ana-emb-sa-h-1.why: The sinus venosus receives blood from the embryonic veins at the caudal end of the straight heart tube. Blood then passes forwards into the primitive atrium.

notes.A: The primitive atrium receives blood from the sinus venosus, placing it just beyond the venous inlet.
notes.B: The bulbus cordis lies at the arterial end and contributes to the developing right ventricle.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle lies between the atrium and bulbus cordis and pumps blood towards the arterial end.
notes.E: The similarly named conus cordis forms ventricular outflow tracts at the arterial end of the tube.

ana-emb-sa-h-2.why: The septum secundum grows down on the right of the septum primum. Its free lower edge forms the rim of the foramen ovale.

notes.A: The thin septum primum supplies the mobile flap that covers the opening on its left side.
notes.B: The septum spurium forms where the venous valves meet near the entry of the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The venous valves form the septum spurium, whereas the rim of the opening belongs to the septum secundum.
notes.E: The septum secundum leaves an identifiable opening through which foetal blood passes into the left atrium.

ana-emb-sa-h-3.why: The ductus venosus carries some oxygenated placental blood from the left umbilical vein towards the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids.

notes.A: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta so blood can bypass the foetal lungs.
notes.B: The truncus arteriosus is the common arterial outlet of the embryonic heart before the great arteries separate.
notes.C: The sinus venosus receives embryonic venous blood at the heart and has no direct shunting role within the liver.
notes.E: The ductus venosus provides the named connection that allows placental blood to bypass much of the hepatic circulation.

ana-emb-sa-h-9.why: The superior and inferior endocardial cushions meet in the common atrioventricular canal. Their fused tissue forms the septum intermedium between the future right and left atrioventricular openings.

notes.A: The foramen ovale is a passage between the foetal atria, above the level of the atrioventricular canal.
notes.B: The septum secundum forms the rim of the interatrial opening on the right side of the atrial septum.
notes.C: The septum spurium arises near the venous inlet from the upper ends of the venous valves.
notes.D: The septum primum grows from the atrial roof towards the cushions and helps partition the atria.

ana-emb-sa-h-10.why: Displacement of the outlet septum narrows the pulmonary outlet and leaves a ventricular septal defect beneath an overriding aorta. The right ventricle hypertrophies under the pressure load. Persistent ductal patency is a separate finding.

notes.B: The aorta overrides the septal defect, allowing it to receive blood from both ventricles.
notes.C: Displacement of the outlet septum leaves a gap between the ventricles immediately beneath the overriding aorta.
notes.D: The displaced outlet septum narrows the right ventricular outflow tract, restricting flow towards the lungs.
notes.E: The right ventricular muscle becomes hypertrophied as it pumps against the obstruction at its outlet.

ana-emb-sa-h-74-77.why: The foetus receives oxygen from the placenta. Preferential flow across the foramen ovale sends relatively well-oxygenated blood to the upper body, while the ductus arteriosus diverts much of the right ventricular output past the lungs.

notes.A: The umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood towards the foetus, while the paired umbilical arteries return blood to the placenta.
notes.C: Among the systemic arteries, the ascending aorta and its arch branches receive relatively oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle.
notes.B: High resistance in the foetal lungs favours flow from the pulmonary artery into the descending aorta through the ductus arteriosus.

ana-emb-sa-h-78-82.why: The foetal atrial septa overlap to form a one-way passage. After birth, increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure and presses the thin flap against the rim.

notes.A: The septum primum grows from the roof of the common atrium towards the endocardial cushions.
notes.B: The septum secundum develops to the right of the septum primum and overlaps its opening.
notes.C: The openings in the overlapping septa are offset, producing an oblique route from the right atrium to the left.
notes.D: The flexible septum primum opens like a flap against the more substantial septum secundum.
notes.E: After the lungs expand, left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure and holds the flap closed.

ana-emb-sa-h-83-90.why: The expanding ventricles develop a muscular partition that initially leaves an opening near the outflow tract. Tissue from the atrioventricular cushions and outflow ridges helps close this opening.

notes.A: Looping positions the cardiac chambers, whereas growth of the ventricular myocardium produces the muscular septum.
notes.B: The muscular septum arises at the floor of the developing ventricles as their walls expand.
notes.C: Tissue from the atrioventricular cushions helps close the remaining gap above the muscular septum.
notes.E: The membranous region is a common site of defects because several developing structures must unite there.
notes.D: The primitive ventricle gives rise to the trabeculated portion that forms most of the left ventricle.

ana-emb-sa-h-91-95.why: The arterial outlet divides to form the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk. Beyond the outlet, selective persistence of the aortic sac and paired arch arteries establishes the great vessels.

notes.A: The third arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal part of the internal carotid artery on each side.
notes.B: The proximal sixth arch arteries contribute to the pulmonary arteries on their respective sides.
notes.E: The right horn of the aortic sac gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk.
notes.C: The distal left sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, joining the left pulmonary artery to the descending aorta.
notes.D: Partition of the truncus arteriosus produces the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk.

notes.A: The distal umbilical arteries become the paired medial umbilical ligaments, which run beside the bladder on the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.B: The ductus arteriosus closes and forms the ligamentum arteriosum between the left pulmonary artery and the aortic arch.
notes.C: The ductus venosus closes and forms the ligamentum venosum within the liver, beyond the course of the former umbilical vein.
notes.E: The vitelline veins form parts of the portal venous system and the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava.

ana-emb-es-9.why: Foetal blood entering the right atrium can push the thin septum primum towards the left atrium. A pressure rise on the left presses this flap against the septum secundum and closes the passage.

notes.A: Endocardial cushions help partition the atrioventricular canal, whereas the flap comes from the septum growing down from the atrial roof.
notes.B: The crista dividens is a ridge that separates incoming blood streams at the rim of the interatrial opening.
notes.D: The septum secundum provides the rim against which the thinner flap closes when left atrial pressure rises.
notes.E: The inferior caval valve helps direct blood towards the foramen ovale from the venous inlet upstream of the flap.

ana-emb-es-119.why: The embryonic outflow tract normally separates into an aorta and a pulmonary trunk. Failure of this partition leaves a single common arterial trunk supplying both circulations.

notes.A: Tetralogy of Fallot involves an abnormally positioned outlet septum, with pulmonary outflow obstruction and an overriding aorta.
notes.B: In transposition there are two separate great arteries, but each connects to the opposite ventricle.
notes.D: A ventricular septal defect is an opening between the ventricles. It often accompanies a common arterial trunk.
notes.E: A patent ductus arteriosus connects an already separate pulmonary artery and aorta through a persistent foetal vessel.

ana-emb-sa-h-38.why: The respiratory bud grows out from the endodermal lining of the ventral foregut. Its epithelium gives rise to the lining of the trachea, bronchi and lung air spaces.

notes.A: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, whereas the respiratory bud arises within the endoderm-lined foregut.
notes.C: Splanchnic mesoderm around the bud forms bronchial cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue around the endodermal lining.
notes.D: Somatic mesoderm lines the body wall and contributes to the parietal pleura surrounding each lung.
notes.E: Extraembryonic mesoderm supports structures outside the embryo, including placental vessels, whereas the lung bud forms within the embryo.

ana-emb-sa-h-39.why: Deficient bronchial cartilage can allow a lobar bronchus to narrow on expiration. Air enters on inspiration but escapes poorly, so the affected lobe progressively expands and compresses adjacent lung.

notes.A: Oligohydramnios can limit lung growth, leaving small lungs with insufficient tissue for gas exchange.
notes.B: Surfactant deficiency increases surface tension and promotes alveolar collapse at the end of expiration.
notes.C: Unilateral agenesis leaves an entire lung absent and cannot account for air trapping within a developing lobe.
notes.E: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula allows aspiration during feeding, while extra lobes alone provide no mechanism for expiratory obstruction.

ana-emb-sa-h-40.why: The respiratory diverticulum normally separates from the dorsal oesophagus as the foregut divides. An incomplete separation can leave a tract connecting the tracheal and oesophageal lumens.

notes.B: Congenital lobar overinflation results from expiratory air trapping, sometimes because an affected bronchus lacks adequate cartilage.
notes.C: Congenital lung cysts arise within the developing airways or lung tissue, away from the tracheo-oesophageal partition.
notes.D: Hyaline membrane disease arises when surfactant deficiency allows alveoli to collapse, usually in a premature infant.
notes.E: Accessory lung lobes result from variations in branching or lobulation within the developing lung.

ana-emb-sa-h-142-145.why: A tracheo-oesophageal fistula allows air or liquid to cross between the airway and the oesophagus. In the common distal fistula, air can reach the stomach and refluxing gastric contents can enter the lungs.

notes.C: Focal lobar overinflation suggests an obstructed bronchus, whereas an open fistula primarily predisposes to aspiration.
notes.A: With a distal fistula, raised airway pressure during crying can drive air through the oesophagus into the stomach.
notes.B: Refluxing gastric contents can travel up the distal oesophagus and through the fistula, causing aspiration and lung injury.
notes.D: Surgical closure separates the airway and digestive tract and prevents continued passage of material through the fistula.

notes.B: The pleuroperitoneal folds help close communications between the developing pleural and peritoneal cavities and contribute to the diaphragm.
notes.C: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, but the partitions that separate it from the pleural cavities develop as named folds.
notes.D: The dorsal mesentery suspends the developing gut from the posterior body wall within the abdomen.
notes.E: The septum transversum forms the central tendon of the diaphragm between the thorax and abdomen.
